html:
Polarization of light
View
Click any red incident E arrow of the starburst to split it into a component along the filter axis (passes) and one across it (absorbed).
Guided demo
Drag to orbit: every E arrow stays in the plane perpendicular to the ray — the starburst is a transverse disk of directions, not a flat fan.

plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 34: The Nature of Light
plan.contextChunk: This figure carries two labeled panels, (a) and (b), each a perspective sketch of a light ray with its electric field vectors. In panel (a), a thin blue line slants from the upper left down to an arrowhead at the lower right and is annotated Direction of ray (of propagation). From one point on that line, eight bold red arrows radiate outward in the plane perpendicular to the ray, evenly spaced and pointing up, down, left, right, and along the four diagonals; four are tagged E with a vector arrow, and the group is headed Random polarization. Panel (b) repeats the same blue ray, drawn longer, with an identical red starburst near its left end. Farther along the ray sits a tan shaded ellipse labeled Polarizing filter by a curly leader and crossed by a vertical double-headed black arrow labeled Axis. Beyond the filter, a single red arrow remains on the ray, vertical and double-headed, labeled E and tied by wavy leaders to Polarization direction and Direction of ray. Setting the many-armed starburst before the filter against the lone vertical arrow after it is the comparison the two panels stage, introducing unpolarized light and the filter that passes only the field component along its own axis.

elements: thin blue straight ray line slanting from upper-left down to lower-right, with a solid arrowhead at its lower-right end (direction of propagation)
starburst of 8 bold red double-ended-looking arrows radiating from a single point on the ray, evenly spaced every 45° in the plane perpendicular to the ray (up, down, left, right, four diagonals)
four 'E' vector labels (with over-arrow) attached to selected starburst arrows in panel (a)
text label 'Random polarization' above the starburst
text label 'Direction of ray (of propagation)' near the lower-right of the starburst in panel (a)
panel caption '(a)'
panel caption '(b)'

tan/orange shaded ellipse (circular polarizing filter seen obliquely) with a darker tan rim and a thin edge/thickness highlight, centred on the ray downstream of the starburst, its face perpendicular to the ray
vertical black double-headed arrow drawn across the face of the filter indicating the transmission axis
curly leader line with text 'Polarizing filter' pointing down to the filter
curly leader line with text 'Axis' pointing to the black double-headed arrow
single red vertical double-headed arrow on the ray beyond the filter (transmitted polarized E field)
'E' vector label beside the transmitted red arrow
curly leader with text 'Polarization direction' pointing to the transmitted red arrow
curly leader with text 'Direction of ray' pointing to the blue ray beyond the filter

interactions.teaches: Contrast between unpolarized light (many equally likely E directions perpendicular to the ray) and light after a polarizer (one E direction only).
interactions.label: View

interactions.teaches: The transmitted polarization direction is set by the filter's own axis, not by the incoming light: rotating the axis rotates the surviving red E arrow with it.
interactions.label: Filter axis angle (0° = vertical)

interactions.teaches: For one chosen incident E direction, only its component parallel to the filter axis passes; the perpendicular component is absorbed.
All E vectors lie in the plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation — rotating the view shows the starburst is a transverse disk of directions, not a flat fan.

demo_steps.title: Unpolarized light
demo_steps.narration: A ray travels from upper left to lower right. Eight red E arrows radiate from a point on it, all perpendicular to the ray and equally likely — this is random (unpolarized) polarization.

demo_steps.title: Insert the polarizing filter
demo_steps.narration: A tan filter disk is placed across the ray. Its transmission axis, the black double-headed arrow, is vertical. Downstream only one red arrow remains, vertical like the axis.

demo_steps.title: Rotate the axis
demo_steps.narration: Turning the filter axis to 45° turns the transmitted E arrow to 45° as well: the filter, not the source, chooses the polarization direction.

demo_steps.title: One incident direction at a time
demo_steps.narration: Click any incoming red arrow: it splits into a component along the axis (passes through, drawn bold) and a component across it (fades out, absorbed).

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Ray: a single straight line of length ~14 world units running from upper-left/back to lower-right/front, direction d ≈ normalize(1, -0.32, -0.45); drawn as a thin tube radius 0.025 in teal-blue #1F7A9B with a cone arrowhead (length 0.5, radius 0.15) at the far lower-right end. Place the origin at the starburst point, located at t = -4.5 along the ray in panel (a) (centred in frame) and at t = -5 in panel (b) (near the left end of the longer ray). Starburst: 8 arrows of length 1.5, shaft radius 0.055, cone head length 0.4 radius 0.16, colour brick red #C0392B, all lying in the plane perpendicular to d, spaced every 45° starting with 'up' = the projection of world +Y onto that plane. Four of them (up, upper-right diagonal, right, lower-right diagonal) carry italic 'E' labels with an over-arrow, offset 0.35 beyond the tip. Filter: flat disk (cylinder, radius 1.3, thickness 0.10) centred at t = +1.5 along the ray with its axis along d, so it projects as an ellipse ~2.6 wide and ~1.6 tall; face fill warm tan #F3D2A0 at ~0.75 opacity with a rim torus in #E8A martin-orange #E09A3E, plus a thin lighter inner outline. Axis indicator: black double-headed arrow of full length 2.2 drawn on the filter face, lying in the filter plane, at angle filterAxisAngle measured from the in-plane 'up' direction (0° = vertical, positive = counter-clockwise as seen from the camera), linewidth ~0.035 with small cones at both ends. Transmitted field: one red #C0392B double-headed arrow, half-length 1.1, centred at t = +5 on the ray, lying in the plane perpendicular to d and oriented exactly along the current filter-axis direction. Labels in dark grey/near-black #1A1A1A sans-serif, attached by thin curly (quadratic-bezier) leader lines: 'Polarizing filter' above the disk, 'Axis' to the upper right of the disk, 'Polarization direction' upper-right of the transmitted arrow, 'Direction of ray' right of the ray's far end, 'Random polarization' above the starburst, 'Direction of ray (of propagation)' below-right of the starburst in panel (a). Panel caption '(a)' or '(b)' centred beneath the scene. Component decomposition on click: for a clicked incident arrow of direction u in the transverse plane and axis unit vector a, draw the parallel part (u·a)a in full-opacity red with dashed projection lines, and the perpendicular part u-(u·a)a in red at 0.15 opacity; transmitted arrow length scales as |cos θ| where θ is the angle between u and a.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the whole scene in a local frame: compute an orthonormal basis (d, e1, e2) from the ray direction once, and place every arrow/disk with a quaternion that maps +Z to d, so all E vectors are guaranteed transverse. Use THREE.ArrowHelper or custom cylinder+cone meshes (cleaner control over shaft radius) for the red arrows; a double-headed arrow is two cones back-to-back on one shaft. Filter disk: CylinderGeometry with transparent MeshBasicMaterial + a slightly larger TorusGeometry ring for the rim so it reads as the tan ellipse from any orbit angle; render with depthWrite false and side: DoubleSide. Labels as CSS2DRenderer HTML divs anchored to invisible marker Object3Ds, with SVG/line-based curly leaders drawn in the overlay layer so they stay legible while orbiting. Toggle between panels by fading opacity of the filter group and the transmitted arrow rather than rebuilding the scene, and extend/shorten the ray tube accordingly. Click picking via Raycaster on invisible thicker cylinder proxies around each starburst arrow. Orbit limited to ±60° azimuth / ±45° elevation from the default three-quarter pose so the figure stays recognisable.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for filter-axis angle: the learner rotates the polarizer axis, and the transmitted red E arrow stays aligned with the selected axis, showing that unpolarized light becomes polarized along the filter direction.
- Toggle between unpolarized and after-filter view: the learner switches from the many-direction starburst to the single transmitted arrow, making the contrast between random polarization and one selected polarization direction explicit.
- Click on a single incoming E direction: the selected red input arrow is isolated, its component parallel to the filter axis is highlighted through the filter while the perpendicular component fades, clarifying component selection for one chosen incident direction.

authoredContext:
The Sun and many other light sources produce waves that have the electric fields in random directions (the figure(a)). Such light is said to be unpolarized, because it is composed of many waves with all possible directions of polarization. Polaroid materials—which were invented by the founder of the Polaroid Corporation, Edwin Land—act as a polarizing slit for light, allowing only polarization in one direction to pass through. Polarizing filters are composed of long molecules aligned in one direction. If we think of the molecules as many slits, analogous to those for the oscillating ropes, we can understand why only light with a specific polarization can get through. The axis of a polarizing filter is the direction along which the filter passes the electric field of an EM wave.

The slender arrow represents a ray of unpolarized light. The bold arrows represent the direction of polarization of the individual waves composing the ray. (a) If the light is unpolarized, the arrows point in all directions. (b) A polarizing filter has a polarization axis that acts as a slit passing through electric fields parallel to its direction. The direction of polarization of an EM wave is defined to be the direction of its electric field.

Figure a shows a slender blue arrow pointing out of the page and to the right that is labeled direction of ray. Eight red arrows emanate from a point on the ray and are labeled as vectors E. These arrows are all in a plane perpendicular to the ray and are uniformly distributed around the ray. They are labeled as representing a random polarization. In figure b, a similar but longer ray is shown with the same red arrows emanating from a point near the left end of the ray. Farther to the right on the same ray is a thin rectangle with six equally spaced vertical slits. This rectangle is labeled polarizing filter. A vertical double headed arrow on its surface is labeled axis. To the right of the filter, centered on the ray, is a single blue double headed arrow oriented vertically that is labeled E and direction of polarization.

The figure shows the effect of two polarizing filters on originally unpolarized light. The first filter polarizes the light along its axis, decreasing its intensity by a factor of 2. When the axes of the first and second filters are aligned (parallel), then all of the polarized light passed by the first filter is also passed by the second filter. If the second polarizing filter is rotated, only the component of the light parallel to the second filter’s axis is passed. When the axes are perpendicular, no light is passed by the second filter.

discrepancies: The vector labels render as "E□" (tofu) instead of E with an over-arrow — the combining arrow glyph U+20D7 does not display, so the single most repeated annotation in panel (a) is broken.

The starburst is noticeably small and visually compressed relative to the teal ray compared to the source, where the eight E arrows dominate the composition and span roughly the same extent as the drawn ray segment.

Source panel (a) shows eight arrows of equal drawn length arranged symmetrically; the generated foreshortened transverse disk yields visibly unequal projected lengths (upper-left/lower-right arrows much shorter), making the fan look lopsided rather than the even 45° star of the original.

Label placement differs: 'Random polarization' sits immediately above the vertical arrow in the source (with its own E label beside it), whereas here it collides visually with the top E label; 'Direction of ray (of propagation)' in the source is under the starburst rather than under the arrowhead.
evaluation.notes: A conceptually strong, genuinely 3D rendition of unpolarized light and a polarizing filter with excellent interactions (panel toggle, axis-angle slider, click-to-decompose with |cos θ|, guided demo), let down mainly by broken E-vector glyphs and a small, visually squashed starburst.
action_items: Replace the 'E⃗' label markup with a reliably rendering vector notation (e.g. an inline SVG/CSS overline-with-arrowhead or 'E' plus a styled span) so the labels read as E⃗ rather than E□.
Increase the starburst arrow length (or reduce the ray extent / tighten the camera framing) so the eight E arrows occupy a comparable fraction of the frame as in the source figure.

Reduce the transverse-plane tilt slightly at the default view (or add a 'face-on' view preset) so the eight arrows read as a near-even 45° star like the printed figure, while still conveying 3D depth on orbit.

Nudge 'Random polarization' and 'Direction of ray (of propagation)' to match the source positions (upper-left of the star, and directly below the star respectively) and keep them clear of the E labels.

feedback.rationale: Concept and interaction structure are sound (concept 5, no plan action items); the issues are implementation details — broken arrow glyphs, starburst scale/tilt, and label placement — all fixable at the generation level.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Ray: a single straight line of length ~14 world units running from upper-left/back to lower-right/front, direction d ≈ normalize(1, -0.32, -0.45); drawn as a thin tube radius 0.025 in teal-blue #1F7A9B with a cone arrowhead (length 0.5, radius 0.15) at the far lower-right end. Place the origin at the starburst point, located at t = -4.5 along the ray in panel (a) (centred in frame) and at t = -5 in panel (b) (near the left end of the longer ray). Starburst: 8 arrows of length 1.5, shaft radius 0.055, cone head length 0.4 radius 0.16, colour brick red #C0392B, all lying in the plane perpendicular to d, spaced every 45° starting with 'up' = the projection of world +Y onto that plane. Four of them (up, upper-right diagonal, right, lower-right diagonal) carry italic 'E' labels with an over-arrow, offset 0.35 beyond the tip. Filter: flat disk (cylinder, radius 1.3, thickness 0.10) centred at t = +1.5 along the ray with its axis along d, so it projects as an ellipse ~2.6 wide and ~1.6 tall; face fill warm tan #F3D2A0 at ~0.75 opacity with a rim torus in #E8A martin-orange #E09A3E, plus a thin lighter inner outline. Axis indicator: black double-headed arrow of full length 2.2 drawn on the filter face, lying in the filter plane, at angle filterAxisAngle measured from the in-plane 'up' direction (0° = vertical, positive = counter-clockwise as seen from the camera), linewidth ~0.035 with small cones at both ends. Transmitted field: one red #C0392B double-headed arrow, half-length 1.1, centred at t = +5 on the ray, lying in the plane perpendicular to d and oriented exactly along the current filter-axis direction. Labels in dark grey/near-black #1A1A1A sans-serif, attached by thin curly (quadratic-bezier) leader lines: 'Polarizing filter' above the disk, 'Axis' to the upper right of the disk, 'Polarization direction' upper-right of the transmitted arrow, 'Direction of ray' right of the ray's far end, 'Random polarization' above the starburst, 'Direction of ray (of propagation)' below-right of the starburst in panel (a). Panel caption '(a)' or '(b)' centred beneath the scene. Component decomposition on click: for a clicked incident arrow of direction u in the transverse plane and axis unit vector a, draw the parallel part (u·a)a in full-opacity red with dashed projection lines, and the perpendicular part u-(u·a)a in red at 0.15 opacity; transmitted arrow length scales as |cos θ| where θ is the angle between u and a.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the whole scene in a local frame: compute an orthonormal basis (d, e1, e2) from the ray direction once, and place every arrow/disk with a quaternion that maps +Z to d, so all E vectors are guaranteed transverse. Use THREE.ArrowHelper or custom cylinder+cone meshes (cleaner control over shaft radius) for the red arrows; a double-headed arrow is two cones back-to-back on one shaft. Filter disk: CylinderGeometry with transparent MeshBasicMaterial + a slightly larger TorusGeometry ring for the rim so it reads as the tan ellipse from any orbit angle; render with depthWrite false and side: DoubleSide. Labels as CSS2DRenderer HTML divs anchored to invisible marker Object3Ds, with SVG/line-based curly leaders drawn in the overlay layer so they stay legible while orbiting. Toggle between panels by fading opacity of the filter group and the transmitted arrow rather than rebuilding the scene, and extend/shorten the ray tube accordingly. Click picking via Raycaster on invisible thicker cylinder proxies around each starburst arrow. Orbit limited to ±60° azimuth / ±45° elevation from the default three-quarter pose so the figure stays recognisable.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure carries two labeled panels, (a) and (b), each a perspective sketch of a light ray with its electric field vectors. In panel (a), a thin blue line slants from the upper left down to an arrowhead at the lower right and is annotated Direction of ray (of propagation). From one point on that line, eight bold red arrows radiate outward in the plane perpendicular to the ray, evenly spaced and pointing up, down, left, right, and along the four diagonals; four are tagged E with a vector arrow, and the group is headed Random polarization. Panel (b) repeats the same blue ray, drawn longer, with an identical red starburst near its left end. Farther along the ray sits a tan shaded ellipse labeled Polarizing filter by a curly leader and crossed by a vertical double-headed black arrow labeled Axis. Beyond the filter, a single red arrow remains on the ray, vertical and double-headed, labeled E and tied by wavy leaders to Polarization direction and Direction of ray. Setting the many-armed starburst before the filter against the lone vertical arrow after it is the comparison the two panels stage, introducing unpolarized light and the filter that passes only the field component along its own axis.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for filter-axis angle: the learner rotates the polarizer axis, and the transmitted red E arrow stays aligned with the selected axis, showing that unpolarized light becomes polarized along the filter direction.
- Toggle between unpolarized and after-filter view: the learner switches from the many-direction starburst to the single transmitted arrow, making the contrast between random polarization and one selected polarization direction explicit.
- Click on a single incoming E direction: the selected red input arrow is isolated, its component parallel to the filter axis is highlighted through the filter while the perpendicular component fades, clarifying component selection for one chosen incident direction.

Polarization of light

Guided demo
Drag to orbit: every E arrow stays in the plane perpendicular to the ray — the starburst is a transverse disk of directions, not a flat fan.
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: The panel-(a) composition is rendered quite small and sits left-of-centre in a large empty canvas, whereas the source crops tightly around the starburst; the figure reads as a small vignette rather than a filling diagram.
The 'Random polarization' label runs into the topmost E-vector glyph (its leader position in the source sits clearly above-left of the vertical arrow, separated from the E labels).
Source shows (a) and (b) side by side in one plate; the generated version shows only one at a time via the View toggle (toggle exists in code, so this is a layout rather than content loss).

In the source the eight red arrows are drawn as flat, uniformly long 2D arrows with prominent heads; in the render the foreshortened transverse disk makes some arrows visibly shorter/thinner than the source's even star, slightly reducing the 'all directions equally likely' read at first glance.
evaluation.notes: A faithful and conceptually strong 3D reinterpretation of the polarization figure — correct teal ray, transverse red E starburst, tan filter with axis double-arrow behind the (b) toggle, and a rich set of genuinely pedagogical interactions (axis slider, per-arrow cos θ decomposition, face-on view, 4-step demo); main weaknesses are the small/off-centre framing and a label collision at the top of the starburst.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are execution details (framing/zoom, label collision, arrow uniformity) that the generator can fix.

interactions.teaches: Contrast between unpolarized light (many equally likely E directions perpendicular to the ray) and light after a polarizer (one E direction only).
interactions.label: View

interactions.teaches: The transmitted polarization direction is set by the filter's own axis, not by the incoming light: rotating the axis rotates the surviving red E arrow with it.
interactions.label: Filter axis angle (0° = vertical)

interactions.teaches: For one chosen incident E direction, only its component parallel to the filter axis passes; the perpendicular component is absorbed.
All E vectors lie in the plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation — rotating the view shows the starburst is a transverse disk of directions, not a flat fan.

demo_steps.title: Unpolarized light
demo_steps.narration: A ray travels from upper left to lower right. Eight red E arrows radiate from a point on it, all perpendicular to the ray and equally likely — this is random (unpolarized) polarization.

demo_steps.title: Insert the polarizing filter
demo_steps.narration: A tan filter disk is placed across the ray. Its transmission axis, the black double-headed arrow, is vertical. Downstream only one red arrow remains, vertical like the axis.

demo_steps.title: Rotate the axis
demo_steps.narration: Turning the filter axis to 45° turns the transmitted E arrow to 45° as well: the filter, not the source, chooses the polarization direction.

discrepancies: The teal ray's arrowhead is nearly degenerate on screen — because the ray direction carries a large depth component the cone is seen almost end-on and reads as a small teal blob rather than the clean arrow tip of the source figure.
The ray segment is much shorter relative to the starburst than in the source, where the line extends well past the arrow cluster on both sides, weakening the 'direction of propagation' read.

In the source the E arrows are drawn in the page plane with roughly even 45° spacing and equal apparent length; in the generated transverse-disk version the arrows foreshorten unevenly (left/right arrows appear shorter), so the starburst is less symmetric than the printed figure (an acceptable 3D interpretation but a visible composition difference).

The 'Random polarization' caption sits far to the left of the vertical arrow rather than directly above it as in the source, so its association with the top E arrow is less clear (no leader line as in the original's implied placement).
evaluation.notes: A faithful and pedagogically strong reconstruction: correct teal ray, red transverse E starburst, tan filter disk with black axis double-arrow behind a panel toggle, plus a genuinely useful slider/click-decomposition/face-on/guided-demo interaction set; main weaknesses are the nearly end-on (blob-like) ray arrowhead, a ray that is too short relative to the star, and slightly uneven arrow foreshortening compared with the printed figure.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are concrete rendering fixes (arrowhead orientation/visibility, ray length, arrow symmetry, caption placement) best handled by the generator.
